{{Short description|Invariant of rings and modules}}
In [[commutative algebra|commutative]] and [[homological algebra|homological]] algebra, '''depth''' is an important invariant of [[ring (mathematics)|ring]]s and [[module (mathematics)|modules]]. Although depth can be defined more generally, the most common case considered is the case of modules over a commutative [[Noetherian ring|Noetherian]] [[local ring]]. In this case, the depth of a module is related with its [[projective dimension]] by the [[Auslander–Buchsbaum formula]]. A more elementary property of depth is the inequality 

: <math> \mathrm{depth}(M) \leq \dim(M), </math>

where <math>\dim M</math> denotes the [[Krull dimension]] of the module <math>M</math>. Depth is used to define classes of rings and modules with good properties, for example, [[Cohen-Macaulay ring]]s and modules, for which equality holds.

== Definition ==
Let <math>R</math> be a commutative ring, <math>I</math> an ideal of <math>R</math> and <math>M</math> a [[finitely generated module|finitely generated]] <math>R</math>-module with the property that <math>I M</math> is properly contained in <math>M</math>. (That is, some elements of <math>M</math> are not in <math>I M</math>.) Then the <math>I</math>-'''depth''' of <math>M</math>, also commonly called the '''grade''' of <math>M</math>, is defined as 

: <math> \mathrm{depth}_I(M) = \min \{i: \operatorname{Ext}^i(R/I,M)\ne 0\}. </math>

By definition, the depth of a local ring <math>R</math> with a maximal ideal <math>\mathfrak{m}</math> is its <math>\mathfrak{m}</math>-depth as a module over itself. If <math>R</math> is a [[Cohen–Macaulay ring|Cohen-Macaulay]] local ring, then depth of <math>R</math> is equal to the dimension of <math>R</math>.

By a theorem of [[David Rees (mathematician)|David Rees]], the depth can also be characterized using the notion of a [[regular sequence (algebra)|regular sequence]].

=== Theorem (Rees) ===

Suppose that <math>R</math> is a commutative Noetherian [[local ring]] with the maximal [[ideal (ring theory)|ideal]] <math>\mathfrak{m}</math> and <math>M</math> is a finitely generated <math>R</math>-module. Then all maximal [[regular sequence (algebra)|regular sequence]]s <math>x_1, \ldots, x_n</math> for <math>M</math>, where each <math>x_i</math> belongs to <math>\mathfrak{m}</math>, have the same length <math>n</math> equal to the <math>\mathfrak{m}</math>-depth of <math>M</math>.

== Depth and projective dimension ==

The [[projective dimension]] and the depth of a module over a commutative Noetherian local ring are complementary to each other. This is the content of the Auslander–Buchsbaum formula, which is not only of fundamental theoretical importance, but also provides an effective way to compute the depth of a module. 
Suppose that <math>R</math> is a commutative Noetherian [[local ring]] with the maximal [[ideal (ring theory)|ideal]] <math>\mathfrak{m}</math> and <math>M</math> is a finitely generated <math>R</math>-module. If the projective dimension of <math>M</math> is finite, then the [[Auslander–Buchsbaum formula]] states

: <math> \mathrm{pd}_R(M) + \mathrm{depth}(M) = \mathrm{depth}(R).</math>

== Depth zero rings ==

A commutative Noetherian local ring <math>R</math> has depth zero if and only if its maximal ideal <math>\mathfrak{m}</math> is an [[associated prime]], or, equivalently, when there is a nonzero element <math>x</math> of <math>R</math> such that <math>x\mathfrak{m}=0</math> (that is, <math>x</math> annihilates <math>\mathfrak{m}</math>).  This means, essentially, that the [[closed point]] is an [[embedded component (algebraic geometry)|embedded component]].

For example, the ring <math>k[x,y]/(x^2,xy)</math> (where <math>k</math> is a field), which represents a line (<math>x=0</math>) with an embedded double point at the origin, has depth zero at the origin, but dimension one: this gives an example of a ring which is not [[Cohen–Macaulay ring|Cohen–Macaulay]].
